section.title: The Seventh Seal and the First Trumpets
section.sectionRationale: The seventh seal, delayed since chapter 6 while chapter 7 comforted God's sealed people, finally opens, and instead of an immediate vision it produces silence and then seven trumpets, nested inside it just as the seals themselves once nested inside the scroll. This chapter carries the narrative from that dramatic silence, through the incense offered with the prayers of the saints, to the first four trumpet judgments and the eagle's warning of three woes still to come, forming one coherent movement before the fifth trumpet begins the first woe in chapter 9.
section.thesis: When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, heaven falls silent, and then the prayers of the suffering saints, joined with incense at the golden altar, are hurled back to earth as the trigger for the first four trumpet judgments, a fraction of creation struck in each, while an eagle's warning cry announces that far worse woes are still to come.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the silence in heaven and the prayers of the saints offered at the golden altar; the first four trumpets, striking the earth, sea, waters, and sky in turn; and the eagle's cry of threefold woe over what remains.

units.label: The silence and the prayers of the saints

verses.text: When the Lamb opened the seventh seal, there was {{sige|silence}} in heaven for about half an hour.
And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and they were given seven trumpets.

Then another angel, who had a golden censer, came and stood at the altar. He was given much {{thymiama|incense}} to offer, along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne.
And the smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of the saints, rose up before God from the hand of the angel.
Then the angel took the censer, filled it with fire from the altar, and hurled it to the earth; and there were peals of thunder, and rumblings, and flashes of lightning, and an earthquake.

units.label: The first four trumpets
units.note: a third of the earth, sea, waters, and sky struck

verses.text: And the seven angels with the seven trumpets prepared to sound them.

Then the first angel sounded his trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood were hurled down upon the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, along with a third of the trees and all the green grass.
Then the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea turned to blood,
a third of the living creatures in the sea died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.
Then the third angel sounded his trumpet, and a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven and landed on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.
The name of the star is {{apsinthos|Wormwood}}. A third of the waters turned bitter like wormwood oil, and many people died from the bitter waters.

Then the fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun and moon and stars were struck. A third of the stars were darkened, a third of the day was without light, and a third of the night as well.

And as I observed, I heard an eagle flying overhead, calling in a loud voice, “{{ouai|Woe}}! Woe! Woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the trumpet blasts about to be sounded by the remaining three angels!”

sige.gloss: Silence, stillness. After chapters of thunderous worship and terrifying judgment, heaven itself falls silent for about half an hour, a deliberately unnerving pause before the next, more intense sequence of judgment begins, drawing every reader into breathless anticipation of what is coming.

thymiama.gloss: Incense, the fragrant offering burned at the golden altar. Here it is joined directly with the prayers of the saints, the same image used already in Revelation 5:8, showing that the accumulated prayers of God's suffering people are treasured before God and become, in His timing, the very occasion He uses to answer them with judgment on their behalf.

apsinthos.gloss: Wormwood, a bitter plant used in the Old Testament as a picture of bitter judgment and the poisonous fruit of unfaithfulness. The star named Wormwood turns a third of earth's fresh water bitter and deadly, echoing the prophets' warnings that a people who turn from God are given bitterness to drink.

ouai.gloss: Woe, a cry of dread and lament pronounced over coming disaster. The eagle's threefold cry marks the last three trumpets as woes distinct in intensity from the first four, preparing the reader for judgments that press harder on human beings directly rather than on the natural world alone.

basic.context: The Lamb finally opens the seventh and last seal, and instead of a new judgment there is silence in heaven for about half an hour. Then an angel offers incense together with the prayers of God's suffering people at the golden altar, and that same angel hurls fire from the altar down to earth, unleashing thunder, lightning, and an earthquake. Seven angels then begin to sound seven trumpets. The first four strike a third of the earth, the sea, the fresh waters, and the sky in turn, and an eagle flies overhead warning that three even worse woes are still to come.
basic.hermeneutics: People debate what the half hour of silence means and how literally to read a third of creation being struck, and, more broadly, whether these trumpet judgments describe first century upheavals, patterns across history, a future tribulation, or timeless symbols of divine judgment on a rebellious world. What is not in doubt is the pattern the chapter establishes: the prayers of God's suffering people are directly tied to the release of these very judgments, God's answer to His people's long cry for justice.
basic.originalLanguages: Heaven's response to the opened scroll is first sige, silence, an unnerving stillness before the storm. Then thymiama, incense, is offered together with the prayers of the saints, the same prayer imagery already introduced in chapter 5. The third trumpet's star is named apsinthos, Wormwood, a bitter plant long used as a picture of judgment's poison. And the eagle's cry of ouai, woe, three times over, marks a clear escalation in what is still to come.
basic.typology: The golden altar of incense fulfills the tabernacle's altar where Israel's prayers rose to God. The trumpets recall the trumpet blasts of Sinai and the priestly trumpets calling Israel to battle and worship. And the plagues of hail, fire, blood, and darkness directly echo the plagues God sent on Egypt, now unleashed on a wider, cosmic scale against an unrepentant world.
basic.christ: It is the Lamb who opens the seventh seal, setting in motion everything that follows in this chapter; the trumpets exist only because He has first unsealed the scroll. The prayers gathered at the altar are the same prayers of the saints already pictured in chapter 5 as belonging to the Lamb's worship scene, tying His sovereignty over history directly to His care for His praying, suffering people.
basic.god: God receives the prayers of His suffering people as a precious, fragrant offering, not as background noise; He answers them, in His own timing, not merely with comfort but with real, world-shaking judgment on the evil His people have suffered under. Even in judgment God shows restraint, striking only a third of creation in each of these first trumpets, leaving room for repentance before worse woes arrive.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 30:1-8 establishes the golden altar of incense in the tabernacle, the pattern behind this scene. Exodus 19:16-19 pictures trumpet blasts accompanying God's terrifying appearance at Sinai. Exodus 7 through 10 describe the plagues of hail, fire, and blood on Egypt, directly echoed in these first trumpets. Joel 2:1 calls for the trumpet to be blown as a warning of the coming Day of the LORD.
basic.oneStory: From Sinai's trumpet blasts to Egypt's plagues of hail and blood, the Bible has long shown that God announces His judgment with dramatic signs and answers the cries of His oppressed people with real intervention in history. This chapter gathers that pattern into Revelation's unfolding vision, showing that the prayers of the suffering church are never lost, but are treasured before God's throne and become, in His perfect timing, the very occasion of judgment on the evil His people have endured, even as He warns that the worst woes are still ahead.

context.literary:
The chapter has a hinge in the middle and a fork at the end. Verses 1 to 6 are the sanctuary scene: silence, seven angels receiving trumpets, and an angel at the altar with a censer. Verses 7 to 12 are the trumpets themselves, and verse 13 is the eagle's cry that turns the reader toward the three that remain. The structure is the one the seals taught us, four then a pause then three, so that the reader already knows what the eagle means by 'the remaining three'.

The seventh seal opens onto nothing, and then onto everything. The silence is not the vision, it is the intake of breath before the vision. Having read of a sealing in chapter 7 and the sweep of the seals before it, we expect a final judgment, and instead the scroll is opened to reveal seven angels with trumpets. The seventh seal contains the seven trumpets, as the scroll had contained the seven seals, in the way a nest of boxes holds one inside another. The seventh trumpet will in turn contain the seven bowls, Revelation 11:15 and 16:1. This telescoping is one of the main structural clues of the book.

Within the section there is a deliberate ring. Verses 3 to 5 tell of fire, thunder and an earthquake going out from the altar, and the same cluster of sounds comes at the climax of each cycle, Revelation 8:5, 11:19 and 16:18. The incense scene is the pivot that explains why the trumpets sound, because they are the answer to what was just offered. And the trumpets are told in a clipped, repetitive style, each with a 'third' of something. The word 'third' echoes through verses 7 to 12 with almost the force of a drum.

The eagle in verse 13 is the one voice in the chapter that speaks to the reader in direct terms: 'Woe! Woe! Woe!' It points forward and sets up the pause before the fifth trumpet, so that the chapter ends with dread suspended and not yet resolved.
context.historical:
The first thing that the first hearers would have recognised is the trumpet. In Israel the trumpet, the ram's horn or the silver trumpets of the priests, was the signal of worship, of war and of God's appearing. It blared at Sinai, Exodus 19:16, led the march around Jericho, Joshua 6:4, called the people to arms and to the feasts, Numbers 10:9 and 10, and heralded the day of the LORD, Joel 2:1. To hear that seven angels were given trumpets was to hear that God was about to act, in battle and in judgment.

The incense belongs to the daily worship of the temple. Each morning and evening a priest burned incense on the golden altar in the holy place while the people prayed outside, Exodus 30:7 and 8 and Luke 1:9 and 10. The incense carried the prayers up in the people's imagination, as Psalm 141:2 says, 'May my prayer be set before You like incense'. On the Day of Atonement the high priest took a censer of coals from the altar into the holy of holies, Leviticus 16:12 and 13. John's readers who had known the temple, or had heard of it, would see the heavenly scene as the true sanctuary that the earthly one pointed to. The Jerusalem temple lay in ruins if John wrote after AD 70, and the vision tells believers that the true altar is not gone but in heaven.

The judgments themselves have a clear ancestry in the plagues of Egypt. Hail and fire, Exodus 9:23 to 25, water turned to blood, Exodus 7:20 and 21, and darkness, Exodus 10:21 to 23, are named in the trumpets in some form. The first readers would have heard that the God who delivered Israel from Egypt was again acting against an empire that enslaved His people. And for those who lived near the sea in the great port cities of Asia Minor, the loss of a third of the ships and the poisoning of the waters touched their livelihood.
context.canonical:
The silence belongs to a small but recognisable family of texts. Habakkuk 2:20 says, 'let all the earth be silent before Him', Zephaniah 1:7 says, 'Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD, for the Day of the LORD is near', and Zechariah 2:13 says, 'Be silent before the LORD, all people'. In each the silence is the hush that comes before God acts. Half an hour in heaven is the same hush, and the effect is to say that the judgment about to come is God's own doing.

The prayers of the saints return to chapter 5, where the elders held golden bowls full of incense, 'which are the prayers of the saints', Revelation 5:8. The prayers of the martyrs in 6:10 and the golden altar in this chapter are bound together: the cry of the slain is the incense, and the fire that returns to the earth is the answer. Paul says that the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God, Romans 8:26 and 27, and the prayers here rise to God with the help of an angel.

The trumpets draw heavily on the plagues of Exodus. The burning mountain recalls the destroying mountain of Jeremiah 51:25, which God promised to turn into a burnt mountain, a prophecy against Babylon. Wormwood belongs to the covenant curses, where the root that bears poison and bitterness is the idolater, Deuteronomy 29:18, and to Jeremiah 9:15 and Lamentations 3:15. The darkening of the lights echoes Joel 2:10 and Exodus 10:21.

Forward, the trumpet sequence will end with the seventh, which announces that 'the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ', Revelation 11:15. Paul's 'last trumpet', 1 Corinthians 15:52, uses the same image for the end, and Jesus says the angels will gather the elect with a loud trumpet call, Matthew 24:31. The fire, thunder and earthquake at the altar return in Revelation 11:19 and 16:18, each time as a sign that the end is nearer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John means the church to see that its prayers matter. The scene at the golden altar is deliberately placed before any trumpet sounds, and the chain is plain: the prayers rise with the incense, the angel fills the censer with altar fire, and the fire goes down. A church that was small, poor and sometimes hunted is shown that its prayers are not lost in the air but have been received, stored and answered. That would have been among the most important things a persecuted hearer could be told.

He also means to prepare the reader for suffering that is not simple. The judgments are bounded, always a third, and always leaving a remainder, so that the first four trumpets are warnings rather than the end. The reader is meant to see that God's patience is built into the structure, as the remnant gives room for turning. It is only later, in the second woe, that the narrator is blunt about how people respond.

Lastly, the eagle's cry is a pastoral device. It tells the hearers that worse is coming, and it does so in a way that signals God's foreknowledge: the woes are announced before they arrive. Those who belong to the Lord are not meant to be surprised, and they are not meant to despair, since the God who warns is the God who is in charge. The warning is not given to the believers alone, but cries out to 'those who dwell on the earth', a phrase John uses for people at home in a world that has turned away from God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes events seen in a vision. It does not tell anyone to bring about disasters, to read natural events as the trumpets, or to expect that a given earthquake or fire is one of them. A reader who tries to identify the burning mountain with a particular event or the star Wormwood with a person or a nuclear accident is claiming more than the text gives. It uses signs, and a sign points beyond itself.

What does carry across is the pattern of prayer. The scene shows that the prayers of the saints are offered with incense by an angel at the altar before the throne, and it presents that as a fact for believers to rely on, not as a technique to master. We are not told to add anything to our prayers to make them effective. The chapter also gives us a way to understand silence: when heaven is quiet, God is not absent, and the silence may be the preparation for His answer. Believers are not told to expect that God's answers will always come quickly or in the form they hope. They are told that each prayer is received, and that He acts in His time. The chapter also commends the sober view that judgment is a real part of God's dealing with the world and that it comes with warnings.

debates.question: What is the half hour of silence?

views.label: Reverent awe before judgment
views.case: Habakkuk 2:20, Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13 call for silence before the LORD when He is about to act. Heaven, which has been full of singing since chapter 4, goes quiet because the final scroll is being opened. The hush is the right response to the moment the judgments begin.

views.label: A pause for the prayers to be heard
views.case: The silence is followed at once by the scene of incense and the prayers of the saints. Some take the quiet as the space in which heaven listens, so that the cries of the martyrs can be gathered and presented. The silence is then an act of attention, and the trumpets are the reply.

debates.bearing: The two readings are compatible, and many interpreters hold both. In either case the silence is not emptiness but a charged stillness that comes just before God acts. The reader is meant to feel the weight of the moment, whether or not the half hour is a literal measure of time.

debates.question: How are the trumpets related to the seals and the bowls?

views.label: Successive, one after another
views.case: The seventh seal produces the seven trumpets, and the seventh trumpet the seven bowls, so that the sequence runs forward in time and each series is more severe. The fractions grow, a fourth in the seals, a third in the trumpets, and the whole in the bowls, which fits a rising scale.

views.label: Recapitulating, covering the same period from different angles
views.case: The same final marks recur at the end of each series, the lightning, thunder and earthquake of Revelation 8:5, 11:19 and 16:18, as though each is a view of the end. The book also gives overlapping pictures of the same conflict in chapters 12 to 14. On this reading the cycles repeat with growing intensity, and the three sets describe the whole age.

debates.bearing: The nested structure supports both views, which is why serious readers have held each. For the purposes of this chapter the choice does not change the central point, that the trumpets answer the prayers of the saints and that each judgment is partial and bounded.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter opens with sige, 'silence', a word for a hush, and then gives a measured time, hemiorion, 'half an hour'. John does not say what the silence means. He says how long it lasts, and the specific note makes it more disturbing, as in a courtroom when the judge pauses before reading the verdict.

The 'trumpet' is salpigx, and the verb is salpizo, to sound a trumpet. The word appears in the Greek Old Testament for the ram's horn and the straight metal trumpets alike, so the hearers would have heard it as the sound of both worship and war.

The incense is thymiama, and the word is used of the fragrant offering that rose up with the prayers. The same word is in Luke 1:9 and 10 for Zechariah's offering as the people prayed outside. The vessel is the libanotos, the censer, which the angel fills with fire from the altar and then 'hurled', ebalen, to the earth. The verbs show the reversal: the censer that carried incense up now carries fire down, and the same object does both jobs. The prayers go up, and the answer comes down. A small point is that the angel 'was given' much incense, edothe, in the passive that John uses throughout for what heaven permits.

The refrain of the trumpets is 'a third', to triton, which occurs again and again in verses 7 to 12. It is not necessarily an exact fraction. A third is more than a quarter, the proportion of the fourth seal, and less than a half, and it speaks of partial and measured damage with room left for repentance. In the Old Testament thirds fall in Ezekiel 5:1 to 12, where a third of the people die by plague, a third by the sword and a third are scattered, as a picture of judgment on Jerusalem. The trumpets begin by echoing that scene on a global stage.

The third trumpet names the star apsinthos, 'Wormwood', and says the waters became bitter 'like wormwood'. Wormwood stands with poison and the bitterness of judgment in Jeremiah 9:15 and Lamentations 3:15. The bitter plant had no use as drink, and the picture is of life-giving water become the cause of death.

Finally, the eagle. Verse 13 has the 'eagle' flying 'in midheaven', mesouranema, the zenith of the sky, where everyone could see and hear it. The same word is used when an angel flies in the same place in Revelation 14:6 and when the birds are summoned in Revelation 19:17. A later group of manuscripts has 'angel' for 'eagle', but the best witnesses have eagle, and the BSB follows them. The cry 'Woe!' is ouai, said three times, once for each trumpet still to come, and the phrase 'those who dwell on the earth' is the standing label in Revelation for people who are at home in the world's rebellion, as in Revelation 3:10 and 6:10, as opposed to those whose home is in heaven.

typology.type: The golden altar of incense, Exodus 30:1 to 8
typology.fulfillment: Before the veil in the tabernacle stood a golden altar on which incense burned morning and evening, so that a fragrant cloud rose before the LORD all through the generations. Revelation shows the heavenly altar with the prayers of the saints rising in the smoke. The correspondence is the rising incense as the picture of prayer, and Psalm 141:2 makes the link plain. The escalation is that the altar is now before the throne itself, without a veil to stop at, because Christ has opened the way, Hebrews 10:19 to 22. The type falls short in that the earthly priest could offer only for the day, while the heavenly altar serves a prayer life that ends only when the end comes.

typology.type: The plagues of Egypt, Exodus 7 to 10
typology.fulfillment: The first trumpets reuse the plagues of hail, fire, blood in the water, and darkness. In Egypt the plagues were signs of God's judgment on a nation that enslaved His people and a challenge to its gods. The correspondence is the pattern of partial, escalating plagues that give the oppressor a chance to relent. The escalation is that now the plagues fall on the whole earth and the empire is the world's system of idolatry, so that the Exodus becomes a pattern for the final deliverance. The type falls short in that Pharaoh hardened his heart and the plagues did not move him, and Revelation 9:20 and 21 will show the world doing the same.

Seven priests carried seven rams' horns before the ark and blew them as the people marched round the walls for seven days. The walls fell not by human strength but by the word of God. The trumpets of Revelation use the same number and form, with seven angels and seven horns before the throne. The correspondence is that the trumpet sounds as the herald of God's victory over a fortress opposed to Him. The escalation is that the fortress is the whole world order, and the seventh trumpet brings down the kingdom of the world, Revelation 11:15. The type falls short in that Jericho fell in a single day, while Revelation's trumpets unfold with a pause between each sound.

typology.type: The Day of Atonement censer, Leviticus 16:12 and 13
typology.fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement the high priest took a censer of burning coals from the altar and entered with incense, so that the cloud would cover the mercy seat and he would not die. Here an angel takes a censer, adds incense to the prayers of the saints, and then fills it with fire. The correspondence is the censer carried between the altar and the holy place. The escalation is that the heavenly censer both presents prayer and sends judgment, binding the intercession and the verdict together. Hebrews says Christ is the great high priest who has entered the true sanctuary, Hebrews 9:11 and 12. The type falls short in that the priest's work was yearly and never finished.

study.christ:
The chapter does not name Jesus in its verses, apart from the opening words, yet it is saturated with Him. The silence is begun by the Lamb, who 'opened the seventh seal', and everything that follows flows from His act. The trumpets are not the world going wrong without a hand on it. They are the unrolling of the scroll He alone could open, Revelation 5:5 and 5:9, and every trumpet after the first sounds because He has authorised it.

It leads to Christ in the matter of prayer. The angel at the altar presents the prayers of all the saints with incense, and the New Testament gives the reason this can be done: Christ Himself 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near to God, Hebrews 7:25. The altar before the throne is open because of Him, and His blood is what lets prayers rise instead of falling. The angel's service in the scene is real but derived, and the one whose priesthood stands behind it is Jesus, who has entered heaven itself 'now to appear in the presence of God for us', Hebrews 9:24. Paul adds that the Spirit helps us pray when we do not know how, Romans 8:26. A reader who has struggled to pray will see in this chapter that the weakest prayer reaches God through a priest who does not fail.

It leads to Christ by showing what He was refused. Those who dwell on the earth face the trumpets, and the world that has rejected the Lamb receives its warnings. The warnings come in measured fractions, a third and never all, because the Lamb who is Judge is also the one who bore the full wrath for those who flee to Him. Peter says that the Lord is patient, not wanting anyone to perish, 2 Peter 3:9, and the thirds in this chapter are a visible sign of that patience.

It leads to Christ, finally, by contrast with the first Exodus. In Egypt it was Moses who stretched out his staff, and the plagues were signs by a mediator. In Revelation the mediator is the Lamb, and the deliverance He leads is not from a single empire but from the whole age of death. What He did on the cross dealt with the real enemy, and the trumpets mark the days between that victory and its public display. We must be careful not to read each judgment as a coded portrait of Christ. The chapter points to Him by the priestly work of intercession and by the authority of the opened scroll, and it should not be stretched further.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who listens. The prayers of 'all the saints' are given a place at the golden altar, and the smoke of them rises before Him. Whatever God's people have asked in the dark, in the cell or the sickbed or the cry of the oppressed, is not lost. His attention is personal and detailed, and the picture of incense is a picture of a sweet fragrance, so that prayer, even mixed with tears and complaint, is a thing God receives as an offering. This is a more tender doctrine than 'God hears' alone, because it says what He does with what He hears: He carries it to the altar and acts.

He is the God who acts in answer. The fire that was on the altar goes down in the censer. The same altar that took the prayers sends the judgments. Judgment in this chapter is not an arbitrary outburst but a response, and the doctrine that results is that God's justice is bound to His covenant love. The world suffers because the God who loves His people will not ignore what has been done to them.

He is the God of measure. The word 'third' marks every blow. God does not end the world in one stroke, but sets limits, leaves a remainder, and gives time. This is not weakness, since He could do otherwise, but patience in the strict sense, a power held in check for a purpose. Jonah's complaint about God was that He was 'gracious and compassionate' and slow to anger, Jonah 4:2, and the trumpets show the same character at work against the unrepentant: He strikes in warnings, so that those with ears may hear.

He is the God who warns. The eagle announces the woes in advance. There is a kind of mercy in the announcement, for a God who intended only to destroy would not give notice. The prophets had the same role, and Amos says that the Lord does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets, Amos 3:7.

And He is the God before whom silence is the right response. When heaven goes still, that is a lesson in awe. A reader who has grown used to speaking to God easily is reminded that He is also the Holy One before whom the earth is told to be quiet. The proper worship in this chapter is both the incense and the hush, the prayer offered in confidence and the stillness that knows who it addresses. The God who can be asked boldly is the God who can also be waited on in silence.

crossReferences.note: The LORD is in His holy temple, and all the earth is told to be silent before Him. The half hour of silence in heaven is the same reverent stillness, said of the heavenly temple, and it signals that God is about to act.

The prophet commands silence before the Lord GOD because the Day of the LORD is near. The hush at the seventh seal is the same kind of silence, a pause that comes just before the day of judgment breaks.

The psalmist asks that his prayer be set before the LORD like incense and his lifted hands like the evening offering. This verse is the key to the image of the incense rising with the prayers of the saints, since it is how a believing Israelite understood the altar.

The high priest takes a censer full of burning coals from the altar and incense within the veil, so that the cloud covers the mercy seat. The angel's censer, incense and altar fire recall this scene of access and atonement before it becomes the vehicle of judgment.

The LORD sends thunder, hail and lightning on Egypt. The first trumpet's hail and fire recalls this plague, and the link tells the reader that the God who judged Egypt for oppressing His people is acting again for His suffering saints.

The Nile turns to blood, the fish die, and the Egyptians cannot drink the water. The second and third trumpets, with the sea turning to blood and the rivers poisoned, follow this plague and enlarge it from one river to a third of the sea and waters.

God says He will feed the people wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink. The star Wormwood of the third trumpet draws on this judgment, which was spoken to Judah for idolatry and now falls on a world that has done the same.

The LORD speaks against the destroying mountain that devastates the whole earth and promises to make it a charred mountain. The burning mountain thrown into the sea in verse 8 echoes this oracle against Babylon, setting the trumpets as judgment on the world's oppressive power.

The elders hold golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. Chapter 8 returns to that image and shows what comes of it, so the prayers offered in the throne room are the same prayers whose answer begins to fall.

The seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ. It shows where the first four trumpets are going, since they warn of a kingdom that is about to be taken from those who hold it unjustly.

The Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets. The eagle's warning of woes to come follows this principle: God announces beforehand what He will do, so that His people are not taken by surprise.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world made with order and light, and the first trumpets begin to undo it. The first day's light is dimmed by a third, the waters of the second and third days are fouled, the earth's green grass and trees are burned. The sequence runs in the opposite direction to Genesis 1: it is a de-creation in miniature, a loosening of the order God set up. John does this on purpose. The creation was made good and given to human beings to rule, and when they rebel, the world that was made for them begins to be shaken by their sin.

The Egypt story, in the same way, was the first great rescue of a people from a world power, and its plagues become the vocabulary of the final rescue. Exodus tells how God heard the groaning of His people, Exodus 2:24, remembered His covenant, and came down. The prayers at the golden altar are the same groaning in a later age, and the trumpets are the same hearing. The pattern that runs from Egypt to Revelation is that God hears the cry of the oppressed and then acts.

The chapter belongs to the middle of the book and the middle of history: after the cross, where the Lamb won, and before the end, where He will reign. It is the time of the church on earth, the time of prayer and waiting. The believers who are told 'rest a little while longer' in the fifth seal here see what happens to their prayers while they wait. They rise, they are mixed with incense and they are returned as fire.

The end of the chapter looks forward. The eagle announces that the story has further to go, and the trumpet sequence will end with the declaration that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of Christ, Revelation 11:15. That is the point at which the creation made in Genesis and spoiled by sin is given to its rightful King. The new creation of Revelation 21 and 22 then restores what the trumpets disturbed: no more sea that is poisoned, the river of the water of life, and a city that needs no sun, since the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:23. The prayers that rose as incense in chapter 8 are answered by a world in which, at last, nothing needs to be prayed against.

sermon.title: The Prayers of the Saints and the End of the World
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly on Revelation 8:1-5, tracing the silence in heaven and the offering of the saints' prayers at the golden altar, arguing that the prayers of God's people are the very instrument God uses to bring about the trumpet judgments that follow, the exact turning point of this section.

quiz.q: What happens immediately after the Lamb opens the seventh seal?

options.text: There is silence in heaven for about half an hour.
options.note: Verse 1 states this exact and striking response.

options.text: All seven trumpets sound at once.
options.note: The trumpets are given out and sounded one at a time across this chapter and the next, not all together immediately.

options.text: The scroll is fully unrolled and history instantly ends.
options.note: The seventh seal leads into further unfolding judgment, the trumpets, rather than an immediate end to history.

options.text: The twenty-four elders begin weeping uncontrollably.
options.note: The text describes silence, not weeping, following the seventh seal.

quiz.q: What is joined with the incense offered at the golden altar in verses 3-4?

options.text: The prayers of all the saints.
options.note: Verses 3-4 explicitly join the incense with the prayers of the saints, which rise together before God.

options.text: The blood of the martyrs from chapter 6.
options.note: The martyrs' blood and cry appear in chapter 6, but it is specifically the prayers of the saints, not their blood, joined with incense here.

options.text: The names of every nation on earth.
options.note: The text names the prayers of the saints, not a roll call of nations, as what is offered with the incense.

options.text: Nothing; the incense is offered alone.
options.note: Verses 3-4 explicitly state the incense is offered together with the prayers of all the saints.

quiz.q: What happens after the angel fills the censer with fire and hurls it to the earth in verse 5?

options.text: Peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake follow.
options.note: Verse 5 lists exactly these dramatic signs following the censer being hurled down.

options.text: Complete silence returns and nothing further happens.
options.note: The opposite occurs; dramatic signs of judgment erupt immediately after the censer is hurled down.

options.text: The seven trumpets are taken back from the angels.
options.note: The trumpets are not withdrawn; they are prepared and then sounded in the verses that follow.

options.text: The four living creatures are destroyed.
options.note: The living creatures are not harmed in this scene; the judgment falls on the earth through thunder, lightning, and earthquake.

quiz.q: What portion of the earth, sea, and sky is affected by each of the first four trumpets?

options.text: A third, repeated consistently across the first four trumpets.
options.note: Verses 7-12 repeatedly specify 'a third' affected in each trumpet judgment.

options.text: The entirety of the earth, sea, and sky, with total destruction.
options.note: The judgments are severe but explicitly limited to a third, not total destruction, in this set of trumpets.

options.text: Only a small, unspecified area near Jerusalem.
options.note: The text specifies a measured fraction, a third, of the whole earth, sea, and sky, not merely a local area.

options.text: The judgments affect no physical creation, only human hearts.
options.note: The text describes literal, physical effects on earth, sea, waters, and sky, not merely an inward or spiritual judgment.

quiz.q: What does the eagle announce in verse 13?

options.text: Three woes are still coming upon the earth's inhabitants from the remaining three trumpets.
options.note: Verse 13 records the eagle's threefold cry of woe over what is still to come.

options.text: That all judgment has now ended.
options.note: The opposite; the eagle warns of greater woes still ahead, not an ending of judgment.

options.text: That the redeemed multitude from chapter 7 will now suffer these trumpet judgments.
options.note: The woes are aimed at 'those who dwell on the earth,' language Revelation uses for the unrepentant, not for the sealed and redeemed.

options.text: That the seventh trumpet will bring no further consequence.
options.note: The eagle's warning specifically anticipates worse woes still to come from the remaining trumpets, including the seventh.

questions: Heaven fell silent before the next wave of judgment began. Where in your own life might God be asking you to be still and wait rather than rush ahead?

The prayers of the saints were treasured before God's throne and became part of His unfolding purposes. How does this shape the way you think about the prayers you have prayed that seem, so far, unanswered?
God's judgment in this chapter struck only a third of creation, leaving room for repentance. Where has God shown you restraint and patience rather than the full weight of what your sin deserved?
The eagle's cry warned of worse woes still to come, giving people time to turn back to God. Who in your life needs that same honest warning, spoken in love rather than fear?

This chapter ties dramatic judgment directly to the prayers of suffering believers. What would it look like for you to keep bringing your honest cries of 'how long' to God, trusting Him with both the waiting and the answer?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes that the phrase is literally 'became wormwood,' describing the water's transformation into the bitter plant's likeness rather than a mere flavoring, underscoring the totality of the judgment on these waters.

The Greek can be read as the angel offering incense 'with' the prayers of the saints or offering incense that itself represents the prayers of the saints, closely paralleling the golden bowls of incense already identified as the prayers of the saints in Revelation 5:8.

Some manuscripts read 'angel' rather than 'eagle' flying overhead; the reading 'eagle' is well attested and fits the image of a bird crying out a warning from high in the sky, visible and audible to all below.
